## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷakāliṅgajātaka* (Ja 301) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection, translated into English under the title *King Kāliṅga* [SuttaCentral]. According to its traditional framing, the Buddha delivered the tale while staying at the Jetavana monastery concerning the admission of four female ascetics to the monastic life, opening with the incipit phrase "Open the gate" [SuttaCentral].

Scholars note that narrative elements in the text belong to stock Buddhist motifs; Bhikkhu Sujato observes that the narrative includes the standard episode of Jain wanderers, a rose-apple branch trampled by boys, and a philosophical inquiry posed by Sāriputta—a stock sequence identical to accounts preserved in the commentarial traditions of the nuns Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā and Nanduttarā [Sujato 2011]. The Pali text and its commentary were edited in Latin script by V. Fausböll in the third volume of his edition of the Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies external cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. Within the Pali tradition, DharmaNexus identifies 6 text-reuse matches (encompassing 703 characters, with the longest corresponding to segment range §4.1–4.6) between the root text and the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
